doc.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Civil liberties, family and the press
title: Black Power era, LeRoi Jones and Jewish-black relations in jazz
summary: He says his relations with black musicians did not change, regrets the divisions and criticizes Baraka's 9/11 poem.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I was going to ask if, in a sense, LeRoi Jones / Amiri Baraka is a tragic figure, almost like a Paul Robison, but I decided not to ask that. But I say that as a lead-in to the following question about the schism in the wake of the Black Power movement of the ’60s and the relationship between Jews/white/blacks as it was evinced in the jazz world that you were part of, and how – because you knew Max, and you knew . . .
Right, and when he was married to the Jewish woman, I guess.

So how did you and your jazz peers – let’s say Dan Morgenstern and Martin Williams and the handful of you who we’ll call peers – how did they and how did you experience – what was the difference between your relation with blacks 1957 and 1967, after Stokely Carmichael and Huey Newton and all that? What did it do to the jazz world?

I can’t speak for Dan and the others. But again, being a journalist writing about a wide range of things, there was no difference, because they knew me. They knew what I wrote. If we had disagreements, we talked them out. But it was disheartening to see the divisions going on, but not surprising, because anger clouds judgement. It was Jews who helped finance the beginning of the NAACP. And the people who were killed in Mississippi – [Michael] Schwerner and – they were Jewish.

Yeah. But these things manifested themselves in jazz for a time. Some jazz people even took umbrage at the Freedom Now Suite, saying that jazz shouldn’t get involved in this kind of racial propaganda, even if it was for the right reason. But you can’t tell people what to think or what to say. When Amiri Baraka had that poem which more than implied that there were no Jews when 9/11 happened, because they had been given instructions apparently from Tel Aviv to stay away, that showed me that LeRoi had grown stupid. But I didn’t want to censor him. I did think making him the poet of New Jersey was kind of bizarre, but all that did was show how foolish the legislators in New Jersey were.
